events.title: As AI CEOs clash over regulation, a new culture war is brewing
events.summary: Welcome to Eye on AI. Beatrice Nolan here. In today’s issue: The battle lines in AI regulation are forming. OpenAI discloses more hacking incidents. The King hosts an AI safety summit. The public is getting worried about AI safety. Before we get to today’s AI news—please consider joining us at the inaugural Fortune AIQ Summit at the New York Stock Exchange on Oct. 1: Spend the afternoon with senior executives from companies on the Fortune AIQ 75 list and explore how you can scale your AI experimentation and translate investments into measurable business value. Jeremy will be leading discussions alongside co-hosts, Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell and Live Media Editorial Director Andrew Nusca. Apply here to attend . OK, moving on. The battle lines in the fight over AI regulation are being drawn. In the last few days, what has traditionally been a fairly niche argument about AI safety has become something much more complicated: a culture war. It’s largely panning out like this. On one side is Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, in a rare moment of somewhat unity. Amodei has called for frontier AI companies to slow down where necessary, open the door to independent evaluators, and coordinate around common safety standards. Altman has broadly endorsed the suggestions and said OpenAI will also commit to having independent evaluators inside the company.  On the other are Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who have rejected the premise that new AI regulation is needed. Huang said this week that safety and speed are not in conflict, and that the industry does not need new laws or regulations. Zuckerberg made a similar case, arguing that AI companies already have powerful commercial reasons to build aligned systems, avoid harms that could bring legal liability, work with outside evaluators, and delay releases when they are not ready. In a long post on X, Zuckerberg said that the market could discipline AI companies. People will not use agents that behave in ways they do not want, he said, so trust and alignment will become a competitive advantage. Additionally, labs that do not take safety seriously will fall behind, while those whose systems cause harm will face serious liability. Meta, he said, delayed shipping its Muse agent for several months to focus on security and safety for this reason. Who gets to write the rules? These aren’t the only voices against the proposals put forward by Amodei and those urging for more AI regulation. Cohere, a Canadian AI lab, published a response this week arguing that a safety regime built around a small group of dominant Silicon Valley companies could become “a cartel by any other name,” particularly if they received an antitrust exemption to coordinate around rules other developers would have to follow. Cohere cofounder and CEO Aidan Gomez instead called for an evidence-based risk framework, mandatory transparency, independent testing tailored to a system’s actual capabilities, and assurance mechanisms free from conflicts of interest. “I think we absolutely need regulation,” Joelle Pineau, Cohere’s chief AI officer, told me. “That’s going to be part of the social contract.” As AI enters workplaces and people’s daily lives, she said, people need to understand its properties and feel confident that it is being used safely. “There has to be a level of trust, and the regulatory system is about keeping people safe and instilling trust. So, totally believe in it.” But like Gomez, Pineau warned that the companies building frontier systems should not become the sole authors of the rules governing them. “What we worry about,” she said, “is that there’s a small set of labs that both get to build the technology and set the rules.” Labs like Anthropic and OpenAI should help inform policy, she said, but there should be more people around the table. “To be setting the rules and to do it in a way that excludes other voices from even deploying the technology, let alone setting the rules, that’s the problem,” Pineau said. “If you need to set your rules in a closed room with a small set of very powerful players, you’re not doing so in the interest of citizens.” A culture war Zuckerberg and others have been taking their view on AI regulation directly to President Donald Trump for some time, according to new reporting. The Wall Street Journal reported this week that Zuckerberg, Huang, and Elon Musk had separately contacted Trump last month to oppose an effort to create an industry-funded AI oversight body, modeled in part on the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority. The proposal, put forward by Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis, would have created a standards body funded by the industry. However, the Journal reported that Zuckerberg, Musk, and Huang worried it would concentrate further power in the hands of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind—the three companies most likely to shape its rules. In the end, Trump did not move forward with the idea. Trump, for his part, has made his position clear. He has dismissed calls for an AI slowdown, framed regulation as a threat to America’s competition with China, and said the main guardrail the country needs is a “high IQ president.” Rather than engage with the question of how AI systems should be tested and governed, the administration and its allies have increasingly turned the issue into a culture war. Effective altruism, or EA—a philosophical and philanthropic movement that aims to use evidence and quantitative reasoning to identify the most effective ways to improve people’s lives—has found itself at the center of that. The movement became closely linked to AI safety because some prominent EA-aligned funders, researchers, and organizations have focused on the possibility that highly capable AI systems could create extreme or even existential risks. The movement has made headlines before—particularly after its association with disgraced FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried. Now, it’s firmly back in the spotlight. For example, the New York Post published a cover story this week with the headline: “Meet Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s handpicked super-woke globalists he thinks will save us from an AI apocalypse.” The paper focused on Amodei’s proposal that external evaluators from the nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research, or METR, should be able to inspect advanced AI systems and development processes. On Monday, the Department of War’s Office of the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering also weighed in posting : “Americanism, not effective altruism. The United States will continue to be AI DOMINANT!” While it is probably a good thing that AI safety and regulation are getting more attention than ever, the growing polarization around them is likely to make a sensible debate—let alone any meaningful new rules—harder to achieve. events.title: Customer Data Permanently Lost in Iran Strikes on Amazon Data Centers
events.summary: Half a year after Iranian drone strikes knocked out multiple Amazon data centers, the US tech company has acknowledged the permanent loss of some customer data that was hosted in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates. Amazon Web Services was “unable to restore access to the resources and data” hosted in some of the war-damaged data centers, according to an AWS dashboard update posted on September 15. The development was first reported by Reuters and suggests that the Iranian strikes inflicted catastrophic damage on the data centers. Customer data was irretrievably lost in one of three AWS availability zones in the United Arab Emirates region, specifically the mec1-az2 availability zone. Each availability zone is serviced by one or more Amazon data centers. The company is still working on “recovering regional resources” and restoring resources hosted in the other two availability zones in the United Arab Emirates. The AWS update described ongoing work to replace “affected infrastructure” and promised to update customers on a restoration of services in the coming months. But the destruction was apparently even more widespread for the data centers in the Bahrain region, because Amazon said it was unable to restore access to resources and data across all three availability zones there. “The damage to our infrastructure spanned multiple availability zones and exceeded what our regional and multi-AZ services are designed to withstand,” the AWS update said. The company had already suspended customer billing in the affected AWS regions in Bahrain and the UAE and has spent the past six months attempting to restore normal operations. The Iranian drones first struck the Amazon data centers on March 1 in the opening days of the ongoing war that began with US-Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28. AWS immediately urged customers to migrate resources to other cloud regions and use remote backups to restore any “inaccessible resources.” The cloud service also reportedly issued $150 million in customer credits following the initial Iranian strikes in March. A follow-up Iranian strike focused on Amazon’s data centers in Bahrain on April 1. The latest AWS update acknowledged this “disruption” of a second availability zone in the Bahrain region in April but described most affected customers as having already followed the company’s recommendations to migrate their cloud computing workloads elsewhere. On July 24, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched yet another strike using missiles that specifically targeted a remaining Amazon data center structure in Bahrain. That damage was independently confirmed by satellite imagery. “We remain committed to supporting our customers in Bahrain in the long term and will share a further update in early 2027,” the latest AWS update said. Meanwhile, the US-Israeli war with Iran has since spiraled into a broader regional conflict and growing global energy crisis because of attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. One of the few silver linings has been the surging interest worldwide in renewable power generation, such as solar rooftop panels. This story originally appeared on Ars Technica . events.title: Judge steps in as Kennedy Center demolition fears grow
events.summary: Trump officials must give 30 days' written notice before making any changes to the Kennedy Center "including but not limited to any ' demolition '" of the main building, a federal judge ruled Thursday. Why it matters: The ruling reinforces an earlier injunction blocking the Kennedy Center from closing for its planned renovation, after President Trump and administration officials raised the possibility of demolishing the building. The ruling allows the center to continue to make "emergency repairs" rather than halt them entirely. Driving the news: District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled Thursday that the defendants must file a "detailed status report, supported by a sworn declaration from a knowledgeable representative of the Kennedy Center, on the 'temporary closure' and emergency repairs described" in the Kennedy Center board's most recent court filing, per a minute order published Thursday. Representatives for the White House and Kennedy Center did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Catch up quick: Trump said on social media Tuesday that the center was going to be closed. Shortly after, an announcement played over the center's loudspeakers telling attendees that it was closed. Legal counsel for the institution initially said someone had improperly triggered a fire alarm, causing the loudspeaker announcement. But when the plaintiff's staff attempted to enter Wednesday during regular operating hours, security denied them entry and said the building was closed for interior construction and safety reasons. The staff member said she later saw workers using forklifts to bring in additional construction-style gates and watched a forklift carrying permanent fencing repeatedly strike the building's structural pillars. Context: Trump was recently pictured looking at a markup reading, "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED." He told reporters on Wednesday that the Kennedy Center had been bleeding money before he "got involved." "For the Trump administration, for me, to get involved and to take that on long term, and to carry it, or to raise money to carry it, I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition." "Because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down. It's in very, very bad shape. ... You see steel falling down. You see plaster falling off ceilings. ... It's been very badly maintained for 25 years." Zoom in: Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) has been in a legal battle with the administration since the center's board, made up of Trump appointees, began making changes, including adding the president's name to the building's facade. Judge Cooper has repeatedly blocked that move, determining that only Congress can change the building's name and that even a small inscription would violate the legislation that christened the building. Trump subsequently announced that the center would close. State of play: Beatty's legal team says it is unclear what construction is underway and has raised concerns that the center could undertake demolition or other work that would make public access impossible and circumvent the court's order. The previous injunction doesn't prevent the center from undertaking renovations and repairs without shutting down. But Beatty's attorneys say, "the nature of the construction activities and any potential demolition are unclear. Given the unexplained and unlawful closure, it is possible Defendants intend to undertake immediate steps in order to make public access practically impossible for the foreseeable future," the filing reads. events.title: The house where Lizzie Borden's parents were murdered is now a B&B. Take a look inside.
events.summary: Lizzie Borden's former home, where her father and stepmother were found dead. Joshua Chopy/Chopy Media/Brettman/Getty Images Lizzie Borden's former home was sold in 2021 for nearly $2 million. The home's dark past has made it a popular New England attraction for true-crime fans. Now operating as a B&B, the home has eight bedrooms and furnishings from the 1800s. In December 1892, Lizzie Borden was arrested on suspicion of killing her father and stepmother with a hatchet in their Fall River, Massachusetts, home. Nearly 10 months after her arrest, Borden was acquitted of the crimes, in part because prosecutors lacked physical evidence linking her to the killings. No one else was charged in connection with the murders, and more than a century later, the case remains unsolved. The crime has inspired countless adaptations , including Netflix's "Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story," the fourth installment of Ryan Murphy and Ian Brennan's anthology series, which premieres September 17. While the story continues to draw audiences, the Borden home has become an attraction in its own right. Last listed for sale in 2021 for $2 million, the property now offers ghost tours and operates as a bed-and-breakfast, with rooms starting at $259 a night. Take a look inside the site of one of America's earliest true-crime stories. The Borden family house is in Fall River, Massachusetts. Google Maps Fall River is about 52 miles south of Boston, near the border between Massachusetts and Rhode Island . Andrew Borden was a well-to-do businessman. Brettman/Getty Images According to the Lizzie Borden House's bed-and-breakfast website, although Andrew Borden was born into a prominent  New England  family, he grew up middle-class. He began his career as a carpenter and cabinetmaker, later amassing a considerable fortune through a mix of real estate investments, mill ownership, and banking. At the time of his death, his net worth was reportedly over $300,000, equivalent to roughly $10 million today, according to the website. Andrew carefully selected their Massachusetts home. Joshua Chopy/Chopy Media The house was built in 1845 and purchased by Andrew Borden in the 1870s, local news outlet WJAR reported . Borden chose the home in part for its practical location — a short walk from his Main Street businesses in a bustling part of town —according to the Borden bed-and-breakfast's website. Over a century later, the Borden home has become a popular tourist attraction. Joshua Chopy/Chopy Media Donald Woods and Leann Wilbur operated the Lizzie Borden Bed & Breakfast Museum for more than 15 years before selling it in 2021. Lance Zaal, founder of US Ghost Adventures, bought the property for $1.8 million and has continued operating it as an inn and museum, The Wall Street Journal reported. The home looks as though it were pulled straight from the pages of a history book. Joshua Chopy/Chopy Media While some of the home's furnishings have been replaced over the years with replicas, its original doors and hardware remain intact. Period details are scattered throughout the home, including sewing machines, lanterns, and mannequins dressed in floor-length, era-appropriate gowns. The home is spread out over three levels. Joshua Chopy/Chopy Media Altogether, the home occupies a little over 3,600 square feet. The spacious home can be booked in its entirety and accommodates groups of up to 20 people. Floor plans of the home shared with Business Insider show it has 8 bedrooms and 3.5 bathrooms. Joshua Chopy/Chopy Media The second and third floors are almost exclusively devoted to living quarters. All of the bedrooms have floral wallpaper, ornate dressers, and large wooden headboards. For an additional $30, guests can also arrange to have an axe placed on the beds. Most of the bedrooms are on the second floor, and some are on the third. Joshua Chopy/Chopy Media The primary bedroom includes an en suite bathroom with a tub, according to The Seyboth Team , the brokerage that handled the property's most recent sale. You can stay in one of the home's rooms for $249 a night. The interior of rooms in the Lizzie Borden Museum. Joshua Chopy/Chopy Media Though the home operates as a bed-and-breakfast, it also remains a museum and tour site. Guests staying more than one night must vacate the property between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m. This is the John V. Morse Suite. Joshua Chopy/Chopy Media This room is where Abby Borden was found after her murder. Eerily, a photograph of Lizzie Borden hangs in the bedroom. According to the bed-and-breakfast's website, guests have reported paranormal experiences in rooms throughout the home. This was Andrew and Abby's bedroom. Joshua Chopy/Chopy Media It's the only suite in the entire home that has its own bathroom. The kitchen is located on the first floor. Joshua Chopy/Chopy Media The home has an old-fashioned wood-burning stove that certainly looks like a throwback to the 1800s. It also has modern appliances like a coffee maker and a dishwasher. Joshua Chopy/Chopy Media Despite modern appliances, the room still feels historical. The first floor has several rooms dedicated to entertaining. Joshua Chopy/Chopy Media At first glance, this unassuming sitting room appears rather ordinary. But it conceals a dark history: Andrew Borden was killed here while sitting on the large black couch. There's a less eerie space for entertaining. tk Joshua Chopy/Chopy Media For couples drawn to the home's spooky history, the Borden house hosts several weddings each year. This room would make an intimate setting for a cocktail hour. The home also has a separate gift shop. Joshua Chopy/Chopy Media The gift shop sells items including a Lizzie Borden coloring book, a collector's miniature hatchet, and a mug modeled after Lizzie's mug shot. events.title: Fear and loathing in Trump's Miami backyard over immigration crackdown
events.summary: Staring into the camera, Rep. Maria Salazar cut a new campaign ad that told President Trump what so many of her fellow Hispanic Republicans in Miami are saying: Immigration crackdown has gone too far. Why it matters: The anger at Trump over heavy-handed immigration enforcement is palpable in Miami-Dade County, and there's mounting political worry among Republicans across the state that it could cost the GOP in the midterm elections. Zoom in: A bellwether, Miami-Dade is Florida's most-populous county, which Trump flipped to the Republican column in 2020 and 2024 thanks to strong Latino support , especially among Cuban Americans. "Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar says in her ad. "The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today." Trump carried her district by 15 points two years ago. Today, she's tied in polls with newscaster Eliot Rodriguez, a fellow Cuban American, who said her new ad was a sign of desperation. A Trump adviser told Axios: "I'm getting the Trumpiest Cubans sending me videos from Miami of guys getting busted at places like the gas station, for no apparent reason." By the numbers: In Miami-Dade, 62% of the county's 1.3 million registered voters are Hispanic. They account for 76% of the registered Republicans. 63% of Hispanic voters said they supported "deporting illegal immigrants" while 34% were opposed to them, according to a poll conducted last month by a GOP pollster and shared with Axios But those numbers switched when it came to how deportations were being carried out: Just 29% were in favor; 58% were opposed. "The support is just evaporating. The economy sucks and ICE is just out of control," said the pollster, who's from Miami. "People feel they didn't sign up for this." Yes, but: Trump ran on a platform of mass deportations. He promised to target undocumented criminals, but the president's critics warned that his aggressive immigration push would lead to raids, arrests in the streets, racial profiling and separated families. "There was truth in advertising," the pollster said. Trump last year also began revoking Temporary Protected Status for as many as 1.3 million people across the country, some of whom first received the TPS designation in 1998. "Temporary means temporary," a White House official told Axios, noting that President Biden had allowed millions into the country under TPS and a new program that Trump reversed. Ground zero for the Miami-Dade fear and loathing is in Doral. Trump owns a prized golf course there. It's also nicknamed "Doralzuela" because of the large Venezuelan population. Businesses were hit doubly hard last year when Trump canceled TPS for Venezuelans: Legal workers lost the authorization to work, once-legal residents fled, and those who are still there are in hiding or constantly getting picked up by federal agents. "Our sales have dropped 70%. We spend hours empty," Katia Rios of Pipo Burgers, told CBS Miami on Wednesday. Doral Mayor Christi Fraga, a Republican, has been besieged with complaints and has tried to distance herself from the Trump administration. "I don't agree with the way things are handled," she told CBS. Zoom out: Salazar's Republican congressional colleague from Miami, Mario Diaz-Balart, has a district that stretches from Doral on Florida's southeast coast to Naples on its southwest coast. "We've been sending this message to the administration for months," he said of Salazar's ad. Diaz-Balart, however, hasn't spoken publicly against the administration because he prefers to work behind the scenes. Republicans say they're not too worried about conservative Hispanic voters switching to vote for Democrats, but they all believe turnout for the GOP will be low, which could affect legislative and congressional contests, and perhaps the race for governor. "Byron Donalds better watch out," a top Republican consultant said of the Republican congressman locked in a tighter-than-expected gubernatorial race against Democrat David Jolly. (A Donalds spokesman said Jolly will lose.) Friction point: Miami's best-known Cuban American political figure, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, has been publicly supportive of the administration's immigration policies, despite the outcry back home. Rubio was identified with bipartisan immigration reform in 2013, when he served in the Senate. Venezuelans have grown increasingly agitated with Rubio and Trump for not voicing support for an election date in Venezuela and for the administration's transactional relationship with its acting president, Delcy Rodriguez, a socialist who came to power after the U.S. ousted strongman Nicolas Maduro on Jan. 3. "There's a growing feeling that Trump just wanted our oil," a Venezuelan Republican activist said. Between the lines: Miami-Dade has one of the country's most-diverse Latino populations. Cuban Americans are the dominant group, but there are sizable communities with roots elsewhere in Latin America. Cuban Americans tend to be the most conservative because of the exile community that swelled after Fidel Castro took power there in the 1959 revolution. Exiles from families who fled leftist oppression or violence in Nicaragua, Colombia and Venezuela also found common cause with Cuban-American Republicans over the years. Now, these South Florida Hispanic communities are grappling with an immigration system that treats them about the same as Haitians in Miami or arrivals from Mexico in more liberal U.S. cities such as Los Angeles. Cubans once enjoyed expansive immigration protections in the U.S. Under Trump, they're being deported in large numbers to Mexico and even countries in Africa. Behind the scenes: Salazar's broadside against Trump followed days of discussions between her office, Diaz-Balart's and the administration over the arrest of Luis Galeano, a Nicaraguan journalist in Miami with an active asylum application. The Department of Homeland Security accused Galeano of overstaying his visa. The lawmakers say his visa should have been paused because of his asylum claim, which stemmed from his critical coverage of Nicaragua's leftist dictator, Daniel Ortega, who confiscated Galeano's property and stripped him of Nicaraguan citizenship. "There has got to be a better way to do this," Diaz-Balart said. "I'm hearing that everywhere."

events.title: McKinsey wants ambitious technologists, not just MBAs
events.summary: McKinsey seeks engineers as AI reshapes consulting Joan Cros/NurPhoto via Getty Images McKinsey QuantumBlack leader Ben Ellencweig said the firm is embracing a more technical talent pool. "Our recruiting changed dramatically in the last few years," Ellencweig told BI. McKinsey isn't the only firm shifting its talent base. EY has also expanded from accountants. Once famous for its ties to business schools, McKinsey is casting a wider net to meet its needs. For decades, an MBA was one of the clearest routes into elite consulting . As AI changes the work firms do for clients, the consulting industry is looking for people who can build technology as well as devise the corporate strategy around it. "Our recruiting changed dramatically in the last few years. We recruit from places we haven't recruited before," Ben Ellencweig, who leads McKinsey's AI arm , QuantumBlack, told Business Insider. "Today many, many of our colleagues are coming from non-MBA backgrounds, and then technology too is kind of the next wave." That includes mathematicians, computer-science PhDs, startup founders without degrees, and people with experience at technology companies. The shift is playing out beyond McKinsey. Job postings from Deloitte, PwC, EY, KPMG, McKinsey, BCG, and Bain fell by about 24% in the year ending May 2026 compared to the year before, according to labor-market intelligence firm Draup. At the same time, AI jobs grew from 1.4% to 5% of their total openings. The number of forward-deployed-engineer openings across the seven firms rose from none to 1,404 in that same period, according to the analysis. Such roles require engineers who can deploy and run production AI systems inside organizations, and also do the client-facing work traditionally associated with consulting. According to McKinsey's current job postings, most of those roles require at least four or five years of computer-related engineering experience. Ellencweig said McKinsey is looking to fill these roles with "curious people" who are excited to work with clients and solve problems through technology, but who also bring deep technical skills. The firm is recruiting from different geographies, schools, and "outside-of-school, non-school backgrounds," he said. In an email to Business Insider, the firm added that it is recruiting through "less traditional pathways," such as   coding programs and bootcamps. QuantumBlack itself has grown from 47 data scientists working with a Formula 1 team to "well above 5,000" AI professionals over the past decade, Ellencweig said. Those workers include data scientists, data engineers, designers, product managers, and product owners. McKinsey rival EY has recently spoken about its own push to widen its talent pool . Ginnie Carlier, EY Americas' chief talent and culture officer, told BI earlier this year that the Big Four firm was once exclusively made up of accountants, but now it also hires engineers, creatives, and technologists. Ellencweig said McKinsey is reinventing itself around technology, including how it hires and how it develops current employees. "I view our entire workforce, the entire McKinsey, including our consultant cohort, becoming very technology savvy," McKinsey's Ellencweig said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Uber employees say AI is doing everything from writing support chat responses to answering questions in Slack
events.summary: Some Uber employees said that they felt AI was one reason behind the company's layoffs earlier this month. Bloomberg/Getty Images Some laid-off Uber employees say that AI was playing a bigger role in their day-to-day work. They used AI tools to respond to customer service messages and answer questions posted in Slack. Uber said its latest layoffs were about reducing "management layers" and didn't mention AI. At Uber, AI does everything from answering employees' questions in Slack to writing the response you get when you message customer service during a ride. Six recently laid-off employees who spoke with Business Insider pointed to several ways that AI became more prevalent in their jobs over the past few months. Some said that they were prompting AI to do substantial portions of their work. Uber declined to comment for this story. Earlier this month, the company laid off about 3,300 people, including all of the employees Business Insider spoke with for this article. CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said at the time that the layoffs aimed to cut "management layers" and reduce the number of teams where managers had as few as one or two direct reports. Khosrowshahi didn't cite AI as a motivation in a memo announcing the layoffs. At the same time, the employees who spoke with Business Insider said that the company has pushed ahead with implementing AI in a wide variety of uses. One employee said that in the weeks before being laid off he was using an AI tool that reduced the time it took to do his job to one-fifth of what it used to be. "AI definitely feels like the dynamite under the bridge for a lot of us," the employee said. 'Don't be using ChatGPT to do your work for you' A laid-off employee in Uber's advertising business said that managers were increasingly urging them to use Gemini and ChatGPT to prepare for client meetings. "We were asked to use AI all the time," the employee said. "It was part of our day-to-day work." In many internal Slack channels, Uber uses an AI chatbot called Genie, which provides "prompt responses with proper citations from Uber's internal documentation," the company wrote in a blog post last year. The chatbot provides answers to questions that employees post, the employee said, providing a lot of guidance that previously came from managers. "If anybody else had an answer for you, then they replied," the employee said. "But it was usually AI replying to us about any questions we had." Another employee who worked in customer service said that they used Glean, a similar tool trained on internal company documents, to respond to help requests from Uber drivers and passengers. The tools were meant to help customer service agents find information, the employee said. They often copied and pasted answers from the tools directly into the chat. "It wasn't what we were supposed to use, but it was a tool available to use when our knowledge base wasn't working," the employee said. Other Uber employees said that their managers cautioned against that sort of AI use. "We're also getting guidance like 'Don't be using ChatGPT to do your work for you,'" Kori X, a former evaluation specialist on Uber's GenAI team said. "I think they're struggling with why they are paying these people if they're just using ChatGPT," X said. Uber saw 'real tailwinds' from AI productivity Another laid-off employee said that they didn't feel pressured to use AI at work. The company took a measured approach to implementing AI compared to other tech companies, this employee said, offering office hours, explaining to employees what AI could and couldn't do, and curbing the use of AI-generated pictures in external communication. Uber previously said it has used forward-deployed engineers in " agentic pods " to identify uses of AI across the company, from finance to HR. Uber started cutting off or reducing credits to services like Claude in the first half of this year, the employee said. Uber executives said around the same time that they had already spent their Claude budget for the year and that the company wasn't seeing productivity gains commensurate with what it was spending on AI tools. In a presentation at an industry conference last week, Khosrowshahi cited some of the same justifications for the layoffs as in his memo the previous week. Uber wanted to "have more doers versus managers," he said, and reduced the number of "micro-teams" where managers had as few as one or two direct reports. At the same time, Uber saw an opportunity with the restructuring to take advantage of "real tailwinds as it relates to productivity, whether it is AI or general productivity technology as well," he said. events.title: Shirt brand owner shares fix to get thousands of Temu dupes taken down
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Lonely Kids Club fashion brand owner shares fix to get thousands of Temu dupes taken down Lonely Kids Club designs were copied on Temu. ( Supplied: Warwick Levy ) Warwick Levy, owner of Lonely Kids Club, found thousands of copies of his T-shirts on Temu. He struggled to use Temu's violation reporting form before discovering a workaround. Mr Levy has shared his solution to help other designers who find copies of their work on Temu. When Warwick Levy learned copies of his T-shirts were being sold on Temu, he did not know how to handle it. The Sydney-based owner of Lonely Kids Club, a genderless graphic tee company, hoped the problem would go away. "It got to a point where our entire website was scraped, and we have thousands of designs … so all our designs were on Temu," Mr Levy said. The copies hurt sales. The bestselling "get in the van" shirt, featuring a drawing of the Healthy Harold giraffe, suddenly became significantly less popular. The Get in the Van shirt is one of the most popular designs. ( Supplied: Lonely Kids Club ) "At the time we thought maybe it's just gone stale. But then once it got removed [from Temu], it picked back up almost immediately," Mr Levy said. Like many other small designers in Australia who have found their work copied by overseas giants , Mr Levy did not have the time or money to take the fight to court, and was unsure what government bodies would be able to support him. "I'm a very small self-funded business without any sort of capital or investors. That sort of thing just didn't feel feasible," he said. He reached out to Temu and was directed to its Intellectual Property (IP) Violation form, but the problems did not stop there. "I spent like half an hour, 40 minutes going through and putting in data and then, right before the end where you then click to submit, it just disappeared. The whole window vanished, and then I lost all my work," he said. "I tried it again, spent another 40 minutes and then, again, it disappeared. "I really stressed out because I was like, 'I've lost my work twice. I feel very helpless in this situation, and I don't know what's going on.'" Warwick Levy operates his business from a studio in Artarmon, Sydney. ( Supplied: Warwick Levy ) Mr Levy launched his business in 2011, working out of his bedroom. He now has a studio-warehouse in Artarmon where he collaborates with artists and has a focus on ethical, local production. "It felt like I let [the artists] down because the work was stolen from my website and so that was my responsibility to remove it," he said. Once Temu began selling copies, Mr Levy got complaints from customers about receiving low-quality garments, not realising they had purchased duplicates. "We actually had one person not that long ago sort of say like, 'Why would I buy this design from you when everyone's selling it?'" Mr Levy said. "I say, 'Well, first of all, it's our design. No-one else is meant to be selling it. Everyone else has stolen it.'" Contact Liana Walker at walker.liana@abc.net.au After struggling to successfully navigate Temu's IP violation portal on different browsers, he found a workaround to complete the form. Mr Levy said he started by having the information needed for the report prepared in a separate document. Then he opened the IP form in an incognito window, signed in and never closed the tab. By acting fast, he was able to get the form through to the final stage. After that, he said it took days before he received a confirmation. Some of the listings Warwick Levy submitted to Temu for violating content. ( Supplied: Warwick Levy ) Mr Levy realised complaining about trademark violation sped up the process, and he said the copies were eventually removed, something that took just over a week. A Temu spokesperson said it promptly removed the listings in question after the Lonely Kids Club's reports were received. "Sellers are required to comply with applicable laws and platform policies, and those found to violate our IP policies are subject to enforcement actions, including listing removal, account suspensions, or permanent bans," the spokesperson said. In the hope of helping other designers, Mr Levy has shared detailed instructions about how to get violating Temu listings taken down on the Lonely Kids Club website, and has since added software to his website to help prevent design theft. Mr Levy said while he still found copies of his work online, it was not at the same scale as Temu. events.title: Why Australia has a 'fuel costs crisis' not a fuel supply crisis when it comes to diesel
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Diesel 'crack spread' filling oil refiners' coffers as Middle East conflict cuts farm margins Adrian Roles says skyrocketing diesel, fertiliser and pesticide prices are making it hard for farmers to stay profitable. ( ABC News: Jostina Basta ) Diesel prices are well above pre-war levels and unlikely to come down. Agricultural businesses are being hit hard with increased costs of fuel, fertiliser and pesticides. Rising transport costs could flow through to the rest of the economy and worsen inflation, according to industry experts. It is a long way from the Red Sea to grain farmer Adrian Roles's property in regional New South Wales, but the Middle East conflict is having a major impact on his harvest. The wheat and sheep farmer said the price of diesel, pesticides, herbicides and even shipping to his property just outside Wagga Wagga had all increased. Crude oil, the base product for diesel, has surged past $US105 per barrel, up from around $70 per barrel before the conflict. The price swings are taking a toll. "So it's costing us, on the bottom line, about 40 per cent of our profitability," he said. For farmers like Mr Roles the pressures from the conflict in the Middle East look likely to continue, according to Commonwealth Bank head of commodities Vivek Dhar. The war's closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world's oil normally flows, has left much of the world scrambling for commodities like diesel. Pipelines that bypass the strait have alleviated some of the pressure but have been damaged in the conflict. Mr Dhar said only about half the amount of crude oil from before the war is being exported from the Persian Gulf. Oil tankers in and near the Strait of Hormuz are being attacked during transit. ( AP/ISNA ) He believed the price of diesel would soon be more than the market would be able to stomach, with attacks on Russia's diesel refineries worsening the global shortage. Refiners are not letting a crisis go to waste, with the profit margin per barrel, known as the "crack spread", increasing from around $24 to $69. Australia is particularly vulnerable to those price swings as it imports around 80 to 90 per cent of its diesel. Farming is a particularly volatile industry with slim profit margins. ( ABC News: Jostina Basta ) Mr Roles, who is also chair of the New South Wales Farmers Grain Committee, said "it's not like we can pass on these additional costs". "We sell into a global commodity market, so we're price takers as well," he said. "We're basically taking the international price." It is not just diesel that is pushing up costs for farmers. The rising prices of fertilisers and pesticides made from petrochemicals has cut into their margins as well. Volatile fuel prices the real problem That cost of rising fuel prices flows into the rest of the economy, and businesses have to pay more to transport their products, Container Transport Alliance Australia director Neil Chambers said. Neil Chambers says the rising costs of transport will make it harder for businesses to ship their products. ( Supplied: Scott Jewell ) "The price [of diesel] has risen dramatically, over 50 per cent, and that puts a great strain on cash flow," Mr Chambers said. He said transport businesses were immediately passing higher fuel prices onto their customers. Diesel price 'deja vu' for grain farmers nearing harvest They don't need oil changes or spark plugs but is it cheaper to run an EV? 'Papa, when will you be home?' The hidden cost of the fuel discount ending Drivers brace for petrol price hikes as fuel excise cut comes to end One example of the pressures is at Butler Freight Services, based adjacent to Australia's busiest container port in Melbourne. Before the conflict, transport companies like Butler would update their fuel surcharge, a fee on top of standard costs, once a month or every few months. "Currently it's once every week. That's because of the volatility in fuel pricing," Mr Chambers said. That means fuel increases are being passed down the supply chain and through to the eventual consumer much more quickly. Track the latest petrol and diesel prices around Australia See what's happening with petrol and diesel prices near you, updated constantly. That is unlikely to change, according to Mr Chambers. "It's going to be a number of years of higher fuel prices," he said. Transportation impacts the cost of almost all goods, so the potential for diesel prices to further drive up inflation is real. Inflation, the speed of price rises, is already above the rate the central bank wants to see, between 2 and 3 per cent a year.

events.title: Oil prices fall as Saudi Arabia reportedly offers more crude via Hormuz after pipeline attack
events.summary: Oil prices fell Thursday as Saudi Arabia shifts some crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz to compensate for the closure of a key pipeline, easing market fears that the outage will cause another major disruption to global supplies. Brent futures, the international benchmark, lost $1.01 to close at $104.82 per barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude shed 52 cents to settle at $101.91. U.S. crude oil is up nearly 2% for the week and has advanced more than 18% for the month. The Saudis are making additional crude cargoes available to Asian refiners through ship-to-ship transfers just outside Hormuz near Oman's Sohar port, sources familiar with the matter told Reuters . Shuttle vessels transport crude through Hormuz and then load it onto tankers waiting outside the strait, which allows these ships to avoid the risk of Iranian attack while sailing into the Gulf. Saudi crude loadings at its Mideast Gulf ports are up so far this month, said Matt Smith, director of commodity research at Kpler. And ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman have risen to 2.7 million barrels per day compared with 1.5 million bpd in August, Smith said. But it is difficult to know whether the Saudis or other Gulf states are behind those transfers, he said. U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNBC on Tuesday that the Saudis have taken "quick action" to export more oil through Hormuz with the assistance of the U.S. military. Earlier this week, the Saudis halted crude loadings at the Red Sea export terminal at Yanbu and canceled some shipments to European customers, industry sources told Reuters. Yanbu has become Saudi Arabia's key route for oil exports since Iran began attacking tankers in the Strait of Hormuz following U.S. and Israeli attacks on the country in late February. The Saudis closed the East-West pipeline late last week after it sustained damage in a drone attack launched from Iraq. The U.S. Energy secretary told CNBC the outage is a "brief and temporary interruption" that "will be measured in days." But independent analysts warn it could take weeks or months to repair the damage. Rapidan Energy expects Saudi crude oil exports to fall by 400,000 barrels per day this month due to the pipeline outage. But lower shipments from Yanbu should be partly offset by higher exports through Hormuz, Rapidan said. "Risk remains skewed toward a larger disruption if the pipeline outage extends past September or Iran, the Houthis, or other proxy groups escalate attacks," Rapidan told clients in a Thursday note.

events.title: Goldman’s top strategist just added hard numbers to his earnings-bubble warning
events.summary: Peter Oppenheimer, Goldman Sachs’ chief global equity strategist, told clients in early August that technology stocks might not have a valuation problem. Instead, they might have an earnings problem. In a note published Thursday, he came back with the receipts. The new report, titled “Competition for Capital,” doesn’t back off the August thesis. It hardens it, tying the risk of an AI-driven “earnings bubble” to a specific mechanism, a specific historical stress test, and a specific near-term trigger that he says is already showing up in this month’s bond-market turbulence. He still won’t say that this bubble definitely exists. But six weeks after first raising the possibility, the hedge is now backed by capex-to-cash-flow data, record credit issuance, and a downgraded near-term outlook on stocks. The August admission In early August , Oppenheimer wrote that “there does not appear to be a valuation bubble, but there may be an earnings bubble” building in technology stocks—a notable concession from a strategist at what one of the Street’s most consistently bullish research shops. At the time, Oppenheimer’s evidence was mostly anecdotal. He pointed to the wild swings in that quarter’s earnings, Microsoft’s stock jumping 17% in a single day on strong earnings, Meta shares falling nearly 10% despite beating estimates, and the equal-weighted S&P 500 outperforming its cap-weighted counterpart by the widest margin since 2009—signs, in his reading, that investors were growing suspicious of how concentrated the earnings growth powering the market actually was. He linked the risk loosely to “more government debt, increased issuance, and persistent inflation” pushing up the cost of capital, without fully spelling out how that connected back to tech earnings specifically. Thursday’s note turns that loose linkage into the central argument. Oppenheimer now says AI infrastructure spending and government borrowing are directly competing for the same pool of capital: private companies raising debt and equity to fund AI data centers, at the same time governments are borrowing more for infrastructure, energy security and defense, all while inflation from higher energy prices pushes policy rates higher too. That collision, he argues, is what’s driving up the global cost of capital—the mechanism that was only implied in August is now the report’s title and its through-line. He backs the argument with sharper numbers: Capital spending among AA-rated technology issuers grew 65% year-over-year in the second quarter, marking the tenth consecutive quarter that aggregate AA capex growth has topped 35%. U.S. convertible bond issuance has reached $135 billion year-to-date, with AI-related borrowers responsible for 44% of total volume. And Goldman’s credit team raised its full-year U.S. investment-grade issuance forecast by $200 billion, to a record $2.3 trillion, with AI-related issuers now accounting for a quarter of all that supply. An independent echo from Apollo Oppenheimer isn’t the only senior Wall Street voice converging on this framing. Five days before his note was published, Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, wrote his own diagnosis , arguing that what used to be a “savings glut” has turned into a “savings shortage. Slok argued that the two-decade regime of ultra-low rates was a function of excess savings chasing too few investment opportunities. “That has now changed,” he wrote. “Today, there are more projects than capital … When projects are abundant and capital is scarce, capital competes for projects, and it competes by demanding a higher return. The return that clears the market is a higher yield.” He offered a rather cute doodle to make his point. Slok’s evidence is already visible in secondary bond markets rather than merely forecast, as he pointed out that spreads on hyperscalers’ longest-dated bonds have widened, and that “most of the paper issued in 2026 trades wider today than where it priced. Investors are still buying. They are just charging more.” He also offered a precise explanation for why long-term rates specifically have moved more than short-term ones—a dynamic Oppenheimer’s own note opens with, citing 30-year German and Japanese yields near zero as recently as 2022. “Data centers, power generation, transmission and government deficits are all long-duration claims on savings,” Slok wrote. “So the competition for capital concentrates at the long end of the curve, which is why long rates have moved more than short rates.” Running the 2008 comparison to its conclusion Oppenheimer’s August note gestured at historical parallels without fully working through them—pointing to 2008 banks, the dot-com bubble of the late 1990s, and Japan’s bubble in the late 1980s as prior instances where earnings, rather than valuations, blew up first. He notes that banks briefly became the largest sector in the S&P 500 in the run-up to the 2008 financial crisis without ever trading at extreme valuations the way tech did in 1999 or Japanese stocks did in the 1980s. Instead, bank earnings were inflated by rapidly rising leverage financing an asset that did experience a genuine valuation bubble: U.S. real estate. When housing collapsed and pushed the economy into recession, bank earnings collapsed with it, even though the stocks themselves had never looked obviously overvalued. He then checks technology against that same model and lists three reasons he thinks today looks different. First, technology profits remain “very robust” and balance sheets are “strong overall,” a contrast with the credit-fueled fragility that eventually undid bank earnings. Second, interest coverage ratios for the aggregate S&P 500 rank in the 99th percentile of the past 20 years, and the median stock’s coverage ratio ranks in the 68th percentile—evidence, he argues, that companies broadly are not over-leveraged the way banks were. Third, demand for AI compute is “accelerating and outstripping supply” rather than sitting atop an asset that’s already inflated, pointing to Microsoft’s stated plan to triple its data center capacity within six years and to Nvidia’s reiterated forecast, delivered at Goldman’s own Communacopia Technology Conference, that the AI total addressable market will reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030. Still, this isn’t a clean bill of health. Oppenheimer wrote: “Any slowdown in profit growth, in an environment of a much higher cost of capital, could put downward pressure on equity prices, reducing confidence in future cash flows across the ecosystem from the hyperscalers to the ‘pick and shovels’ that have been benefiting from the capex

events.title: The AI Slowdown Debate Crashed Salesforce’s Party
events.summary: Decked out in purple and plaid, Gwen Stefani belted her 2002 single “Underneath It All” to a packed conference center in San Francisco on Tuesday morning—but she was just the warm-up. At the end of her performance, Stefani shouted “Dreamforce! Let’s go!” into a checkered microphone before Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff strode into the spotlight. Dreamforce is billed as the world’s largest enterprise software conference but feels more like attending a megachurch—especially this year. Benioff roamed the audience while delivering his Dreamforce sermon, followed by a teleoperated camera on wheels that beamed his face to screens hanging from the cavernous room’s ceiling. Within minutes, he ordered up a graph of Salesforce’s annual revenue, which the company projects will top $46 billion in 2027, thanks in part to demand for its AI-powered products. The audience applauded. But hanging over the whole event was a dark question: Is artificial intelligence really worth risking all our lives for? Between flashy software demonstrations of agents building dashboards, conference-goers watched Silicon Valley leaders debate whether the AI industry should keep barreling ahead or if the government needs to slow AI progress to prevent catastrophic risks stemming from the technology. Last week, AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic and publicly warned that companies racing toward self-improving AI systems were “gambling with our lives.” By the weekend, other Anthropic employees were echoing his concerns, and CEO Dario Amodei was urging world leaders to help “pace the frontier” of AI development. Other AI CEOs then began endorsing the idea, including Amodei’s greatest rival, OpenAI’s Sam Altman. But not everyone is on board with the idea. David Sacks, a White House AI adviser, brushed off Amodei’s suggestions and fears of AI doom as “just another bid for regulatory capture.” President Trump went further this week, calling fears about existential AI risk “ a hoax .” Despite the challenging political environment, Congress is trying to capitalize on the moment and push ahead with legislation to regulate the AI industry . Onstage, 6-foot-5 Benioff towered over Anthropic’s CEO, vigorously shaking Amodei’s hand just before asking for his latest assessment of AI progress. While this is undoubtedly Benioff’s show, Anthropic has become a critical partner helping usher Salesforce into the AI era. “Let’s say you're running a car company, and another car company, not yours, they have some kind of safety incident,” Amodei said, making a not-so-subtle reference to OpenAI’s Hugging Face incident . “Obviously, it's very tempting to attack your competitor,” Amodei added, but the more responsible move is to “organize the rest of the industry and say, what can we do to set standards for everyone?” But the Anthropic CEO was careful to note that pacing the frontier doesn’t mean “freezing the technology in place,” and of course, he took a moment to plug Claude’s integration with Salesforce. Moments after Amodei exited, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang appeared and began downplaying the concerns Anthropic has raised. AI safety effectively amounts to an “engineering problem,” Huang argued, and the companies building AI can simply police themselves. “We don't need any new laws, we don't need any new regulation,” Huang told Dreamforce attendees. “You run as fast as you can, but if you feel that at any given point in time, the company is out of control or the products are not going to be safe, you take a pause.” The debate feels a bit heavy for Dreamforce, but then again, maybe this is the perfect venue for it. As tech executives pitched their various enterprise AI tools, I slipped out of the room, passing the plush mascots and vaguely Hawaiian decorations, to take a call from Sayash Kapoor, an incoming computer science professor at UC Berkeley. Kapoor and Princeton professor Arvind Narayanan are coauthors of the book AI Snake Oil and write a Substack together called AI as Normal Technology . The pair are known for cutting through AI marketing hype while not dismissing the technology’s potential. This week, they published one of their longest essays yet , which tries to make sense of “loss-of-control incidents,” referring to events such as OpenAI accidentally letting its agents hack into Hugging Face. “Part of what we were trying to do in this essay is to move past this false dichotomy to bridge the ground between AI safety and cybersecurity,” says Kapoor. “If you think AI will soon become superintelligent and evade any controls we can put in front of them, of course, alignment seems more important. On the other hand, if you think AI companies have been negligent and avoided taking bog-standard cybersecurity steps, then it’s natural to think that control is what we need to intervene on. I think both of these views have some element of truth in them.

events.title: Why the Federal Reserve is lifting rates now, and what it means
events.summary: About six weeks ago, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh announced that a divided central bank was keeping its key interest rate unchanged WASHINGTON -- About six weeks ago, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh announced that a divided central bank was keeping its key interest rate unchanged. But on Wednesday, the Fed's rate-setting committee unanimously agreed to a rate hike , and nearly all policymakers signaled that a second increase later this year would likely be appropriate. In short, the renewed fighting in the Middle East has pushed up gas prices again. And there are signs the economy is still growing at a healthy pace even as inflation stays stubbornly high . All three factors appear to have pushed the committee from wait-and-see mode to determined action. Yet the Fed's move doesn't necessarily mean Americans will pay significantly higher costs for mortgages or other borrowing in the short-term, because financial markets appear reassured by the Fed's commitment to fighting inflation. On Thursday, the 10-year Treasury yield even slipped a bit, a likely sign of reduced inflation worries among investors. The Fed's increase “alleviates concerns around the Fed taking sticky inflation seriously,” Oscar Munoz, head of U.S. economic research at TD Securities, said. “And that they’re ready to act, not just talk about it but actually act.” The Fed increases the short-term rate it controls to slow borrowing and spending and ideally cool inflation. The Fed's rate can influence longer-term costs such as mortgage rates, but the Fed doesn't directly control them. For months, Fed officials have considered whether higher oil and gas prices from the Iran war would just amount to a temporary hit to inflation. If so, it might not make sense to hike rates: By the time higher borrowing costs started to slow the economy, the gas price shock could be over and inflation would fall back to the Fed's 2% target on its own. But with the Iran war now in its seventh month, Fed officials are no longer counting on it being a temporary shock. At the Fed's previous meeting July 29, its statement said inflation was elevated “in part reflecting supply shocks that have driven price increases in certain sectors, including energy.” But its latest statement Wednesday dropped that reference to supply shocks, and instead noted that consumer and business spending “has been resilient.” And at his news conference Wednesday afternoon, Warsh said, “our judgment about ... the geopolitical situation has changed.” Gas prices, meanwhile, have continued their steady march higher, reaching $4.44 a gallon Thursday, according to AAA. That's 38 cents higher than a month ago. Diesel prices have hit record highs at $6.40, which will push up shipping costs for many types of goods. Whenever the Fed increases interest rates, it raises concerns that higher borrowing costs will ultimately weigh down the economy so much that a recession results. Yet Warsh emphasized that the economy is healthy and has continued to grow despite repeated blows from things like higher gas prices, tariffs, and higher interest rates. Judge blocks adding Trump tribute to Kennedy Center in scathing ruling Twin sisters conjoined at head underwent successful separation surgery: Hospital Man arrested in death of woman found hanging from tree in Mississippi “Our decision comes at a time when the American economy appears to be strengthening,” Warsh said. “New hiring, private-sector earnings, business capital investment — each of these markers has improved in recent months and is pointing in a good direction. “Consider the geopolitical landscape of shocks and uncertainty, and you begin to appreciate the resilience of the U.S. economy,” he added. While the economy may be showing signs of acceleration, stubborn inflation has eroded Americans' take-home pay. Inflation has now risen faster, on a yearly basis, than average incomes for five months, making it harder for Americans to afford necessities such as gas, food, and rent. Warsh said the “least well-off” have the “most to gain” from steady growth and stable prices. If the Fed can get inflation to its 2% goal, when Americans “get their wages, they can put their head above water and deliver real take home pay increases,” Warsh said. President Donald Trump renewed his criticisms of the Fed Wednesday night and called for much lower interest rates, but did not attack Warsh, whom he appointed as chairman earlier this year. That's a big change from Warsh's predecessor, Jerome Powell, who was the subject of repeated personal attacks from Trump, as well as a criminal investigation, which was later dropped. “The board is very hostile. They’re very political. They’re doing the wrong thing. They’re a bunch of politicians,” Trump said, referring to the 12 Fed officials on the central bank's rate-setting committee. “They’re raising rates to make Trump do as bad as they can possibly do.” Yet economists argue Trump's criticisms are misguided.

events.title: Alex Karp says the AI safety debate is really about nationalizing AI labs
events.summary: Alex Karp weighed in on the AI safety debate during a Thursday interview. Sean Rayford/Getty Images Alex Karp argues that AI companies are collecting intellectual property. Karp told CNBC that AI companies could face lawsuits over the intellectual property they collect. He said those liability risks could ultimately force AI labs to seek nationalization. Alex Karp says there's more to Anthropic's plea for government regulation than safety. Palantir's CEO said in a Thursday interview with CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that frontier AI labs like Anthropic are seeking nationalization to protect themselves from future lawsuits alleging they stole intellectual property. "These businesses have to be nationalized because if you don't nationalize them, every single one of my clients is going to sue," Karp said of AI labs. "The obvious solution is America." Karp said some of Palantir's clients have told him that their proprietary business ideas are ending up as training data for chatbots and being exposed to the wider world. "They find out that the competitor next door has all of their output," Karp said. A potential barrage of lawsuits, Karp said, could spur AI companies to seek government protection to shield them from liability. "That model would require severe liability protection, and there's only one institution that can do that: the US government," he said. Karp has previously railed against frontier labs over the issue of data protection. In June, Palantir published a nine-point manifesto urging companies to keep their data in-house, rather than outsourcing to institutions that Palantir paints as untrustworthy. "Transferring that data hands over access to your pre-existing winning plays and yields the means of production for new ones," reads one point in the manifesto. Fears about the safety of AI programs exploded into the mainstream after ex-Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon quit his job earlier this month and issued dire warnings that frontier AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI are " gambling with our lives ." On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay advocating for a coordinated slowdown and warning that recursive development, a process by which AI improves itself, could soon produce rogue AI agents capable of taking over the internet. That essay was signal-boosted by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. In the essay, Amodei said that "all frontier labs should partner with government" to prevent incidents of misalignment among AI models. "Some forms of coordination that would be impactful for pacing are legally challenging, and will require government support," he said. President Donald Trump signaled over the weekend that he was uninterested in regulating the industry. "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" the president said on social media. To Karp, the debate is being framed incorrectly. "This is reported as a regulation , non-regulation movement," Karp said. "That's actually not what this movement is." "The only way to deal with this kind of liability is to go to the government and say, 'nationalize us, please,'" he added. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: SpaceX discusses buying data for AI models from failed start-ups
events.summary: SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk speaking via video conference to delegates at the G-20 Innovation Ministerial summit, in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, US, on Sept 1. Elon Musk’s SpaceX has held internal discussions about buying customer and operational information from troubled or defunct start-ups, according to people familiar with the matter, targeting a more affordable data source to improve its artificial intelligence models. The approach would mirror Google’s offer to purchase business data from Spirit Airlines for artificial intelligence training purposes after the discount carrier wound down operations. The Alphabet company’s US$10 million (S$12.7 million) bid sparked some data privacy concerns, including from former flight attendants. The talks within teams inside SpaceXAI, the company’s AI unit, are informal and may not result in a deal, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the information is not public. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. Musk’s space, satellite communications and AI conglomerate is locked in a heated battle to build more advanced AI offerings that rival the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI as it works to sign up more business customers. Like other AI companies, SpaceXAI, formerly known as xAI, is focused on securing high-quality data sources that can be used to boost the performance of its models on various tasks. The firm is targeting operational data and customer information to train Grok, among other sets, some of the people said. The strategy of using external datasets marks a departure of sorts for SpaceXAI, which has previously relied on data from Musk’s social network, X, as well as a fleet of in-house specialists known as AI tutors to train and refine its artificial intelligence software. SpaceXAI is still using its internal tutors to help engineers make AI systems better at specialised skills such as finance, science and even humour, but the team has gone through a series of exits and strategy changes. SpaceXAI paused hiring for AI tutors, Bloomberg News reported in June, and later swOpped leadership. Jack Garabedian, a staffer that had spent years working at SpaceX’s Starlink satellite-internet service, recently took over the team, replacing college-aged engineer Diego Pasini, Bloomberg previously reported. Since then, Garabedian has worked to quell discontent on the team, establishing processes and meetings as well as clear goals for AI training data, said the people. In an internal newsletter seen by Bloomberg News, the data team highlighted some of its achievements for July, including progress made on a new AI model and coding agent. “None of these land as polished products without the quiet, exacting work of annotation, preference alignment and validation that happens every day on this team,” the newsletter said. While SpaceX’s AI team considers using more outside data sources, it also continues to rely on information from within Musk’s empire, including employees. “We are going to be training Grok on the sum total of all SpaceX information,” Musk told SpaceX personnel during a recent meeting. “It’ll be trained on you.” BLOOMBERG

events.title: College grads shut out of AI-exposed majors since 2022 are ending up in retail and food service instead of the white-collar jobs they studied for
events.summary: In late 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT, and within months the bottom rung of the tech-industry career ladder started to disappear. Graduates who majored in computer science and other AI-exposed fields are increasingly missing out on the jobs they trained for, and a chunk of them are landing behind restaurant counters and retail registers instead, according to two Census Bureau papers. An April 2026 Census paper tracked matched employer-employee records and found that hiring of workers ages 22 to 24 fell sharply in the industries most exposed to AI, while hiring in less-exposed industries held steady. Employment for early-career workers in the most AI-exposed fifth of industries dropped 12% over the ten quarters after ChatGPT’s release. Lee Tucker, one of the coauthors of the paper, said “the decline in hires is the primary cause” of that rate of unemployment, not people losing jobs they already had. That mattered most for one type of graduate. The most AI-exposed industries, Tucker found, cluster heavily around software and information-technology work, which are the very fields computer science and other highly AI-exposed majors are built to feed into. A second paper from last week, also coauthored by Tucker, follows the graduates of the most AI-exposed decile of college majors. Their odds of holding a job one quarter after graduation fell by five percentage points, and full-quarter initial earnings dropped 13% following ChatGPT’s release. A 13% earnings decline is roughly the size economists would expect from graduating into a severe recession—except there wasn’t one, since the rest of the labor market held up fine. It’s lower-paying jobs, not no jobs at all Young grads still need to work and still have jobs, even if they’ve received highly exposed degrees. So the decline in earnings is less about a lack of employment and more about pursuing lower-wage occupations to make ends meet. About half of the earnings loss came from graduates earning less within the industries that did hire them. The other half came from a shift into different industries altogether, mainly lower-wage sectors like restaurants and retail. Together, the papers suggest that a computer science graduate applies for the same kind of entry-level software job an earlier class would have landed easily, finds the posting isn’t there, and eventually takes a job ringing up groceries or bussing tables instead. The more recent paper found the earnings and employment gaps shrink over time but remain substantial for the most AI-exposed majors even years out. The previous one shows hiring volumes had largely recovered by early 2025, but off a smaller base of jobs, meaning the door reopened only partway. What is striking is how long it took for the students to notice: undergraduate computer science enrollment fell 8.4% in spring 2026 from a year earlier, following a 3.6% drop the prior fall. A Goldman Sachs analysis in June found computer science and computer programming enrollment each fell more than 10% in the 2025-26 academic year, the first year Goldman’s economists saw students visibly reacting to AI in their major choices. A Gallup and Lumina Foundation survey cited in that report found that about 42% of bachelor’s degree students had reconsidered their major because of AI. But in the earlier Census paper, hiring data show the market turning within months of ChatGPT’s release. Enrollment data shows students didn’t start abandoning computer science in visible numbers until three years later. Still, that trend shows up beyond the two Census papers. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s ongoing tracker put the underemployment rate for recent college graduates at 42% in the second quarter of 2026, with unemployment for that cohort running at 5.6%, above the national rate. A Strada Institute and Burning Glass Institute analysis found 52% of graduates were working in jobs that don’t require a degree—retail, food service, hospitality, and office administration among them—within a year of leaving school, and 45% were still there a decade later. events.title: Billionaire investor David Einhorn says younger people are too 'impatient' to build wealth or buy a house
events.summary: David Einhorn is the billionaire founder of Greenlight Capital. Bloomberg/Getty Images Hedge fund investor David Einhorn says many young Americans lack the patience to build wealth or save for a house The investor says young people are putting more focused on putting money into speculative investments. Younger Americans are falling behind in homeownership, a trend that's emerged amid the housing slowdown. David Einhorn says younger generations' own habits are holding them back from breaking into the housing market or building wealth. The billionaire founder of Greenlight Capital recently speculated about the reasons younger Americans are falling behind in homeownership . The main reason, in Einhorn's view, is that many young people lack the patience and investment discipline needed to save up for a home, and are funneling their wealth into speculative assets or sports betting. "I sense the younger generation is just more impatient. They'd rather, you know, speculate in crypto or speculate in stocks or speculate on sporting events and try to build wealth by guessing those things correctly," Einhorn said, speaking in a recent episode of Morgan Stanley's "Break the Playbook" series. "And some of them will have some success with that, and others will have less success," he added. Einhorn said younger people are exhibiting a shift in "philosophy," with many wondering why they should front the extra cash to build equity in a home when renting can be cheaper than owning a mortgage . But owning a home still makes sense from a long-term financial perspective, he said, pointing to the potential for home equity appreciation and how a house often serves as a "savings vehicle." " Buying a house and paying off your mortgage over 30 years, you know, that requires long-term patience and discipline, and that might be in short supply," Einhorn said. Younger Americans are less likely to own a home, a trend that has emerged amid a broader slowdown in the housing market driven by high mortgage rates and near-record home prices.
